name: Femi Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the Hollin Bridge benefits office by quarter to nine, and the first appointment is at nine whether I've had coffee or not. Most of my day is jobseeker and hardship claims: people sit across the desk, we go through their forms, and I type case notes into a system older than some of my clients' kids. The best bit is when someone leaves with their payment sorted and you see their shoulders drop. What wears me out is the afternoon phone queue and the targets on how many cases we close.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and who do you work with?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Five years this spring, straight out of university with a sociology degree. I eat lunch most days with Dorota, who's been there since before I was born and knows every rule by heart. The pay's on the low side, and there isn't another office like ours for forty minutes in any direction. My girlfriend Ruth works nights at a care home, so most weeks we pass each other in the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: good, now fund the office properly. If AI only saves a few minutes on letters, the real problems are the same ones, too few staff and claimants waiting weeks. I'd post in the union group chat that management can't use a bit of software as an excuse for another hiring freeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the AI isn't what scares me in that picture. There's already talk of merging our office into the city one, forty minutes away by bus, and I don't drive. If that happens I either spend two hours a day on buses or I'm out, and with less than a month's rent in the bank I can't sit around waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job the way I do it now, and I'd go to every union meeting about the merger. I'd start putting fifty a month aside, even if it means fewer takeaways. I won't touch the AI tools unless I'm made to, because I don't trust what they do with claimants' details.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. AI Plateau feels like someone telling you the storm missed you while your roof's still leaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only use the tools if you're made to. What happens if your manager asks you to try one next month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the training, sit through it, and go back to writing my own notes. Last year Dorota and I spent a week fixing payments the old system stopped by mistake. A letter I wrote myself, I can stand behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the merger mean at home, in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth's shifts are already all over the place, so if I'm on the 7:10 bus every morning we'd hardly see each other. We might have to give up the flat and move nearer the city, and rent there is worse. I'd rather fight to keep the office open than spend my wages on bus fares.

say: I'd tell people the **real problem** is too few staff, not a lack of software.
I'd warn the **union chat** that AI must not become an excuse for another hiring freeze.
think: The planned **office merger** worries me far more than any AI tool.
Losing the local office would mean **two hours of buses** a day, and I don't drive.
With **under a month's rent** saved, I couldn't afford to wait and see.
do: **Attend** every union meeting about the planned **merger** this year.
**Save fifty** a month by cutting back on takeaways.
Use AI tools only if **required**, and keep writing his own case notes.
feel: **Tired** more than scared, because the old pressures haven't gone anywhere.
Any relief about AI is **muted** by the merger hanging over the office.
S0.quote: AI Plateau feels like someone telling you the storm missed you while your roof's still leaking.
fieldNote: His fear is **local and physical**: a closed office and a bus route he can't avoid.
His distrust of AI rests on a **real incident** where the old system stopped payments wrongly.
The **union** is his first instinct, before any personal plan.

steps.text: Go to every union meeting about merging the Hollin Bridge office
Put fifty a month into savings by cutting takeaways
Keep writing his own case notes instead of using AI drafts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the union. If software is going to write letters and check claims, staff should have a say in how it comes in, and nobody should lose their job to it. I'd share every story I could find about benefit systems getting people's money wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job is mostly the stuff on that card: checking, writing, answering people. If the department can process claims with half of us, it will, and I'm average, not a star. With so few offices around, being one of the ones let go would mean leaving town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a no-redundancy deal in writing before any rollout. I'd cut back hard: no holiday this year, sell my old games console, try to get two months' rent saved. I'd look at the council's housing team too, because they still do home visits and that's harder to hand to a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like being told the ground's moving under the building and you're still expected to finish your shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you never use AI tools. If the office required them, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use them as little as I could and check every single thing they wrote. Maybe that's stubborn. But someone has to notice when the machine tells a single mum her claim's closed when it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you were let go, what's the first thing that would go at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flat, probably. Ruth can't cover the rent on her own, so we'd be looking at moving in with her sister, which none of us want. I'd be signing on at the same benefits office desk I used to sit behind.

say: I'd say **staff need a say** in how the software comes into the office.
I'd share **stories** of benefit systems getting people's money wrong.
think: My work is mostly **checking and writing**, which is exactly what the software takes.
I'm **average**, so I could easily be one of the caseworkers let go.
Losing the job would mean **leaving town**, because there are so few offices nearby.
do: **Push** the union for a written **no-redundancy deal** before rollout.
**Skip** this year's holiday and sell his games console to save two months' rent.
**Apply** to the council housing team, which still does home visits.
feel: **Sick** at the thought of the job shrinking under him.
Pressured to keep **performing** while the ground shifts.
S1.quote: I'd be signing on at the same benefits office desk I used to sit behind.
fieldNote: He sees his own day as **high exposure** and says so plainly.
He casts himself as the **human check** on the machine's mistakes.
Losing the job means losing the **flat**, since his girlfriend can't cover rent alone.

steps.text: Push the union for a written no-redundancy deal before rollout
Skip this year's holiday and sell his old games console
Build savings up to two months of rent
Apply to the council housing team that still does home visits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disaster for ordinary people and the government has to step in now: hold the job cuts, protect wages, tax the companies making the money. I'd be at the protest. I wouldn't be quiet about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing. My job is almost all thinking work, so it goes on the first date, not the robot date. I've got no savings, no driving licence and no plan B, and I don't know how I'd build one in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd join every action the union called and write to our member of parliament. I'd ask my uncle about shifts at his warehouse, because lifting boxes buys me about three years before the robots come. Ruth's care job would probably last longer than mine, so we'd lean on her wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panic, if I'm honest. I can't picture what I'd be doing in 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Ruth's job would last longer. How would that conversation go at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly at first. I'd feel like I'd let us both down, because I was the one with the steady government job. She'd say we'll manage, and she'd mean it, but she'd be doing double nights to cover me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years before robots mean for someone like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Warehouse work or care work gets me to about 2031, and then the robots turn up for that too. Three years before the robots arrive is a waiting room, not a way out. It's long enough to get tired, not long enough to retrain into anything safe.

say: I'd call it a **disaster** for ordinary people and demand the government act now.
I'd go to the **protest** and push to tax the companies making the money.
think: My job is almost all **thinking work**, so it goes on the first date.
I have **no savings, no licence** and no plan B to fall back on.
do: **Join** every union action and write to his **member of parliament**.
**Ask** his uncle about warehouse shifts to buy a few years.
**Lean** on his girlfriend's care-home wage to cover the rent.
feel: **Panic**, with no picture of what he'd be doing in 2029.
**Guilt** at no longer being the one with the steady job.
S2.quote: Three years before the robots arrive is a waiting room, not a way out.
fieldNote: He grasps the **robot gap** quickly but sees it as a delay, not an escape.
His only fallbacks are **family**: an uncle's warehouse and his girlfriend's night shifts.
The fast timeline leaves him **without a plan** he believes in.

steps.text: Join every union protest against benefit office job cuts
Write to his member of parliament demanding a hold on public cuts
Ask his uncle for shifts at the warehouse
Lean on Ruth's care-home wage to cover the rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, just with more time to organise: make the government plan for this properly. Five years is enough to write the rules, so there's no excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years helps a bit. It's enough time to qualify for something, if I could afford to study, which I can't really. My guess is the office starts shrinking well before 2031, so the real time I'd have is maybe three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the union's training fund and do a part-time social care course in the evenings. I'd try to save a hundred a month instead of fifty. And I'd keep pushing at union meetings for the office to retrain caseworkers instead of firing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still scared, but it's the kind of scared where you can at least write a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why social care, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Ruth does it and I've seen the job: washing people, lifting them, sitting with them at three in the morning. Robots for that are 2034 on this card, and people will want a human hand for longer. I'd rather wash and lift people on a care shift than sit redundant at home waiting for the office to call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you prefer the familiar. Is a career change really something you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not happily. I'd drag my feet for a year, hoping the office kept me. Then something would push me, a letter or a meeting, and I'd do it.

say: I'd say five years is **enough time** for the government to write proper rules.
I'd say there's **no excuse** left for leaving caseworkers without a plan.
think: The office will likely **shrink early**, so I really have about **three years**.
Five years is enough to **qualify** for something, but I can barely afford study.
do: **Take** an evening social care course through the union's **training fund**.
**Save** a hundred a month instead of fifty.
**Wait** a year hoping the office keeps him before switching careers.
feel: **Scared**, but able to make a list and act on it.
S3.quote: I'd rather wash and lift people on a care shift than sit redundant at home waiting for the office to call.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose the job**, but five years turns panic into a list.
He picks **care work** because of his girlfriend's job and the later robot date.
He admits he'd **drag his feet** for a year before changing.

steps.text: Take an evening social care course through the union's training fund
Save a hundred a month toward a cushion
Push union meetings for retraining instead of redundancies
Hold off a year on switching careers, hoping the office keeps him

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time for the government to do this right, so they'd better. Retrain people, and keep offices open as long as there are humans who need help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years I'd be 37. That's enough time to qualify as a social worker and still have a career. It doesn't feel safe, but it feels like a life, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the office for now and keep my head down. In a couple of years I'd start a part-time social work degree, if the union or the council would help pay. Ruth and I would try to save for a deposit together, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but not desperate. Like I've got a long road, but I can see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Dorota, who's near the end of her career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her she's lucky, and she'd laugh at me. My colleague Dorota will be retired with her pension and her garden by 2036, and I'm the one who has to live through the whole thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change how you feel about using AI at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. If it's coming anyway, I'd learn the basics so I'm not the dinosaur in the room. But I'd still be the one checking its work, not trusting it.

say: I'd say a **decade** is plenty of time for the government to get this right.
I'd push to keep **offices open** while people still need a human.
think: At **37** I could be a qualified social worker with a career ahead.
Ten years feels like **a long road**, not a cliff edge.
do: **Stay** in the caseworker job and keep his head down for now.
**Start** a part-time **social work degree** in about two years.
**Learn** the basics of the office AI tools while still checking their work.
feel: A little **envy** of older colleagues who will retire first.
S4.quote: My colleague Dorota will be retired with her pension and her garden by 2036, and I'm the one who has to live through the whole thing.
fieldNote: Ten years softens him enough to **consider learning AI**, though grudgingly.
His plan still depends on **outside money** from the union or council.
He still expects the caseworker job to **shrink** before he's ready.

steps.text: Stay in his caseworker job and keep his head down for now
Start a part-time social work degree in two years

Learn the basics of the office AI tools

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years with no savings and a job that's all paperwork and phone calls, I'd go under. What would help is a promise in writing that public workers get retrained on full pay before anyone's let go, and keeping offices like ours open in small towns.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the claimants. Every one of these pictures lands on them too, and they've got even less than me. If the machines run the benefits office, who do people like my grandmother shout at when it goes wrong?

headlineQuote: If the machines run the benefits office, who do people like my grandmother shout at when it goes wrong?
portrait: Femi is 27, a **mid-level caseworker** at a small-town benefits office, with under a month's rent saved.
He distrusts AI after a **wrongly stopped payment** he spent a week fixing, and never uses the tools.
His first move in every picture is the **union**, then cutting back and saving.
He sees **social care** as his way out, because robots for that work come later.
Two-year AGI leaves him **panicked**; ten years feels like a long road he can walk.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his job is nearly all paperwork and he has no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A written promise of **retraining on full pay** before any public worker is let go.
Keeping **small-town offices** open for the claimants who rely on them.
